_about: Playable families. All are fictional, written over real history (docs/planning/05_research_pass2.md section 8).
family.grensboer.summary: Grensboer. Plenty of cattle and sheep, little money. Gerrit knows how to handle stock.
story.grensboer.1: Gerrit Badenhorst's first ancestor at the Cape was a German soldier of the Company, who took his discharge in 1712 to farm as a free burgher and married the daughter of a Huguenot family at Drakenstein. Each generation after moved further east with the cattle, looking for grass and water.
story.grensboer.2: Gerrit grew up on the Bushmans River with his father's herds and the Khoikhoi families who worked them. In the war of 1834-35 the farm was raided, the cattle were driven off, and the house was burned. When London gave the new province beyond the Kei back in 1836, Gerrit decided the Colony would never protect his family.
story.grensboer.3: Now he has sold the farm for less than it was worth. With his wife Susanna, their children, old Klaas the voorloper and Klaas's people, he has come to Grahamstown, where the Uys party is gathering to go north.
family.smid.summary: Smid. Repairs the wagon twice as fast and carries iron and spare parts, but the forge makes a heavy load.
story.smid.1: The Kotzés came to the Cape as smiths: Hendrik's great-grandfather mended the Company's wagons at the Castle in Cape Town. The family moved inland with the farmers they served, and Hendrik learned the trade at his father's forge in Uitenhage.
story.smid.2: Hendrik had customers, not cattle. But his customers were leaving one by one, selling up and heading for the Orange River. A trek without a smith, they told him, would leave its wagons broken in the veld.
story.smid.3: So he loaded his anvil, bellows and iron onto the wagon, though the weight worries him, and brought Aletta and the three small children to Grahamstown.
family.jagter.summary: Jagter. A fine shot and tracker with plenty of powder and lead, but restless; the family's spirits start lower.
story.jagter.1: The du Plessis family were Huguenots who fled France for their faith and reached the Cape in 1688. They kept the French name but lost the language within two generations.
story.jagter.2: Barend has spent more of his life on horseback in the veld than at home. He knows the country beyond the Orange from hunting trips: the game, the springs, and the Griqua and Barolong he has traded with for skins.
story.jagter.3: Now the trek leaders want men who know the land ahead, and hunting may feed a family on the road. Hester thinks he loves the veld more than the farm, and she may be right.
family.weduwee.summary: A widow leads her family north. Large herds and loyal herders, but only one grown son to stand guard.
story.weduwee.1: Magdalena Lombard's husband rode out with the burgher commando in the war of 1834-35 and did not come back. For two years she has kept the farm in the Somerset district going, with her eldest son Stephanus and the herders who have worked for the family since before he was born.
story.weduwee.2: Now her neighbours are selling up and going north, and she will not be left alone on the frontier. Women did lead wagons on the trek when their men were gone, and kept their stock, their children and their places in the laager. Some of the trekker men still doubt that a widow can.
story.weduwee.3: She has the wagon, a great flock and the cattle, Stephanus, who is nineteen and a fair shot, and old Dirk the voorloper, who knows every ox by name. She means to show the doubters.
family.mission.summary: A Wesleyan lay missionary family. Good nurses with plenty of medicine and a Barolong interpreter, but little money and few guns.
story.mission.1: Josiah Whitlock came out in 1820 as a carpenter's apprentice in a Methodist settler party. He found his calling at the Wesleyan chapel in Graham's Town, and has spent ten years building chapels and teaching school at the mission stations beyond the frontier.
story.mission.2: In 1833 the Wesleyan missionaries moved north with Moroka's Barolong to Thaba Nchu. The mission there needs a builder and a teacher, and the trekker families passing through will need the mission. Josiah and his wife Hannah have been sent north with their two children.
story.mission.3: Jacob, a Barolong who learned his letters at the mission school, goes with them to interpret, and Piet drives the oxen. Hannah has packed more medicine than food, and Josiah is not sure that was wise.
family.soldier.summary: A Scottish soldier who stayed at the Cape. Well armed and steady on guard, but little money, few animals, and the trekkers are wary of him.
story.soldier.1: Duncan Rennie came to the Cape as a private in a Highland regiment and fought in the frontier war of 1834-35. When his time was up he took his discharge in Graham's Town rather than sail home, married Agnes, a settler's daughter, and drove wagons for the army.
story.soldier.2: He has no land and little money. He could go home to nothing, or north to wherever there is land and work for a man who can shoot and keep watch. The trekkers are wary of a man who wore the King's red coat, but a party on the road needs men who can stand guard.
story.soldier.3: With Agnes and their children Robert and Jean, Willem to lead the oxen and Griet to help with the stock, he has bought an old trek wagon and is going north.
family.predikant.summary: Lay preacher and teacher. A strong nurse and good spirits, but little money and few men to stand guard.
story.predikant.1: No ordained minister of the Dutch Reformed Church went north with the trekkers at first, so the families had to find their own leaders in worship. Daniël Marais is not ordained. He is a teacher and lay preacher, the son of a Huguenot family from the Drakenstein valley who came east to teach on frontier farms.
story.predikant.2: His wife Johanna keeps a diary, as some trekker women did. She writes down the hymns sung at night, the illnesses, the births and the graves.
story.predikant.3: The family is poor in money, but the trekkers will need someone to read the Bible, nurse the sick, and keep the children at their lessons on the road.
family.settler.summary: English settler family. More money and good colonial credit, but the trekkers do not yet trust them.
story.settler.1: In early 1820 Thomas Ashworth, a weaver whose trade the new mills had ruined, sailed from England with his wife Mary and their small children in one of the settler parties. After about three months at sea they landed on the beach at Algoa Bay in April 1820. Ox wagons hired from Dutch farmers carried them inland to a plot in the Zuurveld, now called Albany.
story.settler.2: Rust ruined the wheat year after year. They lived on pumpkins and maize, and Thomas learned to farm cattle, ride, shoot, and speak the Dutch of the frontier. The war of 1834-35 burned their house. Their son William, born at the Cape, knows no other home.
story.settler.3: Now, in April 1837, the Ashworths stand in Grahamstown among the settlers giving a Bible to the departing trekkers. William has decided to go north, and his parents have decided not to let him go alone.
family.trader.summary: English trader. A heavy transport wagon full of trade goods. Good at bargaining, but a tempting target.
story.trader.1: Samuel Pascoe came out from Cornwall in 1820 as a boy of twelve with his father's settler party. The family's farm failed like so many others, and by 1825 his father had given up farming to work as a carpenter in Graham's Town, where tradesmen were scarce.
story.trader.2: Samuel grew up at the market, among wagons from the far frontier loaded with ivory, hides and skins. He worked for a merchant and made his first trading journeys beyond the colonial boundary.
story.trader.3: Now hundreds of trekker families are heading north, and they will need powder, coffee, cloth and iron. Samuel has loaded a heavy wagon with goods from Mr Holland, the Graham's Town merchant, on credit: thirty pounds, ten of it due within the month. With Ellen and little Grace he is going north with the trekkers.
journal.start.trader: Samuel owes Mr Holland of Graham's Town thirty pounds for the trade goods on the wagon. Ten pounds are due this month.
family.hunter.summary: English hunter. Money, guns and horses, but a small party and few oxen.
story.hunter.1: Edward Fenwick was eight when his family came out with the 1820 settlers. While his elder brothers took on the farm, Edward was sent to school in Cape Town and came back with a love of natural history and an old fowling-piece.
story.hunter.2: In 1836 he met the English officer Captain Harris, who was outfitting in Graham's Town for a hunting journey to Mzilikazi's country. Edward has read of the great herds north of the Orange, and he means to see them for himself.
story.hunter.3: He is going north with his younger brother James, two hired men, a light wagon and too few oxen, as a hunter rather than a settler.
